card.hook: You're about 68 metres up on a hill, and the arched Queen Juliana Bridge looks like it was set out just for your phone. The whole harbour spreads out below you, so the climb is worth it.
card.stand_here: Walk to the far west end of the Fort Nassau restaurant terrace. The phone icon on the map sits right there. Face out over St. Anna Bay, with the bridge arching across your view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the bay and the bridge with the terrace in front. Tap 0.5x to squeeze in more of the harbour and the city. Try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the bridge arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line, and let a bit of terrace wall sit along the bottom of the frame so the view has some depth.
card.best_time: Sunset is the popular time here, and the restaurant advises booking for it. The far west end is usually calmer than the busy sunset corner, so it's a good place to take your time.
card.selfie_here: Stay at the far west end of the terrace, facing St. Anna Bay. Use the front camera, hold your phone a little higher, and let the bay and bridge sit behind you. If your front camera has 0.5x, try it to fit more of the view in.
card.rules_and_safety: The road up is steep and a little confusing, and people jog and train on it, so take care and watch for them. Parking is to the right of the entrance. You can walk around the top of the fort, but not into the harbour control area.
card.challenge: Get the bridge arch off-centre and a slice of terrace wall at the bottom, then see if you can keep the refinery out of the shot.
card.good_to_know: The fort was built in the 1790s and finished in late 1797. It has had three names: Fort Republiek, then Fort George under British rule from 1807, then Fort Oranje Nassau from 1816, which most people shorten to Fort Nassau. It later worked as a control tower for the Queen Emma Bridge, and since 1959 it has been a restaurant.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the far west end of the Fort Nassau restaurant terrace. The phone icon on the map sits right there. Face out over St. Anna Bay, with the bridge arching across your view.

card.hook: Somebody fired a cannonball at this fort in 1804, and it's still stuck in the wall. Fort Amsterdam is also the brightest, yellowest backdrop in Willemstad.
card.stand_here: Stand inside the walls of Fort Amsterdam, right at the phone icon on the map, at the mouth of St. Anna Bay. Face the ochre walls and buildings of the courtyard, and walk up to the ramparts when you want the harbour and bay.
card.zoom: Zoom 0.5x in the courtyard to squeeze in the walls and buildings, use 1x for most shots, and try 2x or 5x for details like the church wall (higher zooms depend on your phone). If parked cars sneak into your wide shot, step to one side or frame tighter on a doorway or wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap the yellow wall and slide it a touch darker so the ochre doesn't wash out in bright sun.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light turns warmer on the yellow buildings. They glow against the sky and the water.
card.selfie_here: Find the southwest wall of the Fort Church inside the fort, where the British cannonball is lodged, and stand beside it with your front camera so the historic wall is behind you. Another good spot is the inner courtyard beside the two old cannons, with the fort walls over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the square outside the fort to step back until the fort walls and the Governor's Palace next door both fit in one frame, while you pose in front.
card.rules_and_safety: The courtyard and walls are open to visitors, but the Fort Church and the government offices may be restricted or ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Hunt down the 1804 cannonball, then photograph it with the church wall perfectly straight against your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The Dutch West India Company built the fort in 1634 as a military base and headquarters, and its walls are about three metres thick. Willemstad grew up outside those walls, and the fort still houses the offices of Curaçao's government and governor. It's now part of the UNESCO World Heritage area of Willemstad's inner city and harbour.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand inside the walls of Fort Amsterdam, right at the phone icon on the map, at the mouth of St. Anna Bay. Face the ochre walls and buildings of the courtyard, and walk up to the ramparts when you want the harbour and bay.

card.hook: One minute you're strolling a long, car-free walkway across the bay. The next, the whole thing swings away and you're staring at open water. Locals call it the "Swinging Old Lady", and she's a great poser.
card.stand_here: Stand about 30 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, near Koningin Emmabrug, and face north-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long, low bridge and the water in one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view, then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for the lighting arches or people crossing.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the brightness down to darker if the sky or water looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. If you want to catch the bridge swinging, ask locally or check the official site, because we can't promise a time.
card.selfie_here: Try the Handelskade promenade right beside the bridge's Punda landing. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the bridge and the colourful waterfront buildings over your shoulder. For a different shot, stand mid-span on the wooden planks with the bridge stretching out behind you. Do check on the spot that the bridge really sits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the Otrobanda-side waterfront promenade by the bridge's Otrobanda landing, facing back across the bay so the whole bridge is in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Some reviewers say the bridge can sway or feel unsteady because it floats, so take care when you walk across.
card.challenge: When the bridge starts to swing, stay put and take a before-and-after pair of the same spot: walkway first, then open water.
card.good_to_know: The bridge was built in 1888 and has been renovated several times, most recently in 2005–2006. The lighting arches date from 1955, put up for a royal visit by Queen Juliana and Prince Bernhard. Cars stopped using it in 1974, so now it's just people on foot, and when it swings open, two free ferries carry pedestrians across.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 30 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, near Koningin Emmabrug, and face north-west.

card.hook: Otrobanda isn't one big view, it's a string of small scenes: old restored buildings, bright details, and the bay with Punda across the water. Think of it as a photo scavenger hunt.
card.stand_here: Stand near De Rouvilleweg, about 290 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for most street and waterfront shots, and zoom 0.5x in squares and narrow streets so everything fits. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for rooflines, shutters or the Punda skyline across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon and building edges level, then tap the main building and slide it a little darker so the bright sky and sea don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the buildings. Midday sun is harsh and can bleach out the colours.
card.selfie_here: Head to the colourful steps at the top of Van Lennepstraat, one of Otrobanda's most photographed spots, where the arched Queen Juliana Bridge also comes into view. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and let the painted steps and the view fill the space behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Museums, the fort village and other sites may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find one bright door or shutter against an old wall, then step back and take a wide shot of the same street to show where it lives.
card.good_to_know: Otrobanda means 'the other side' and was founded in 1707. It's part of Willemstad's UNESCO World Heritage listing. The Queen Emma Bridge, nicknamed 'The Swinging Old Lady', links it to Punda, and Rif Fort has coral walls 1.5 metres thick.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near De Rouvilleweg, about 290 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.

selfie_spots.why: Several guides list these painted steps as one of Otrobanda's most photographed spots, so a selfie on them shows the neighbourhood's colour behind you.

card.hook: Forget one big landmark here. Kurá Hulanda is more like a little village of restored walls, doorways and courtyards, and the fun is in picking your frame. It's also a place with a quiet weight, so take your time and be thoughtful with the camera.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Kurá Hulanda Museum, where the phone icon sits on the map, on the old western quayside in Otrobanda. Face one of the restored façades and step back until the whole front fits in with a bit of sky above.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the buildings look the way they do to your eye. In narrow courtyards or lanes where you can't step back, try 0.5x, but keep your phone upright so the walls don't lean. Use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for doorways, signs and details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with the vertical lines so everything stands up straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. Opening times vary between listings, so check the museum's official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the entrance area, in the centre next to the head sculpture whose face is turned toward arriving visitors. Or stand in front of the museum's main façade. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt the phone up so the building fits over your shoulder. Neither spot is guaranteed to put the whole museum behind you, so check the framing on your screen.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed inside the museum, but flash is not permitted, to protect the artifacts. Check the official site for any room-by-room rules, and be thoughtful about photographing other visitors and staff.
card.challenge: Take one shot of a whole façade with a little sky, then find a doorway, shutter or wall texture and see if you can get its lines perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in April 1999, started by the Dutch entrepreneur Jacob Gelt Dekker, who bought and restored derelict buildings on the quay and market. Today it spreads across 15 buildings. It teaches about the Atlantic slave trade and African history in the Caribbean, and it stands on the old quayside where slave ships once arrived, close to the site of the slave market.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Kurá Hulanda Museum, where the phone icon sits on the map, on the old western quayside in Otrobanda. Face one of the restored façades and step back until the whole front fits in with a bit of sky above.

card.hook: Rif Fort's walls are about 1.5 metres of coral stone, and from a distance they look every bit that stubborn. Pale and heavy, with open water and sky all around, they make a very good first photo of Willemstad.
card.stand_here: Stand near Pater Euwensweg, about 400 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. It's roughly 6 minutes on foot to the fort, so use this spot for the wide view and walk closer for details.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the fort with its surroundings. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for wall details and waves, or 0.5x if you get close and want walls and sky together.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale wall, then drag the slider a little darker if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its texture.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the stone than midday. Check where the sun is on the day, because it decides which side of the fort is lit.
card.selfie_here: Walk through the very thick archway to the outer side of the fort and pose among the oversized cannons. Use the front camera (try 0.5x) and hold it low-ish, so the walls and fountain courtyard fit behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the square outside the fort, where the fortress walls and the palace across from them fit in one frame, with you standing in front of the walls.
card.rules_and_safety: Rif Fort now holds shops, restaurants and entertainment, so parts of it may have set opening times or rules. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Fill the whole frame with wall texture, then sneak in just one wave or a sliver of sky and see if your friends can guess where you are.
card.good_to_know: Rif Fort is a 19th-century fort at the mouth of Sint Anna Bay, on the Otrobanda side of Willemstad. It once held more than 56 cannons, and today its old walls shelter Rif Fort Village with restaurants, bars and shops. Otrobanda dates from 1707 and is part of Willemstad's UNESCO-listed historic centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Pater Euwensweg, about 400 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. It's roughly 6 minutes on foot to the fort, so use this spot for the wide view and walk closer for details.

card.hook: Picture a whole street dressed like a box of pastel crayons, with water lapping right beside it. That's Handelskade, and it's tough to take a dull photo here.
card.stand_here: Head to the spot near Trompstraat and stand about 120 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-west and take your first shots from here.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole street in one frame, but keep your main subject away from the edges, where buildings can look stretched. Use 1x for a natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a few façades.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, then line up the water's edge with a horizontal line and keep the building edges parallel to the vertical ones.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and warmer colour on the painted walls. Midday sun can be harsh and bleach the colours out.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Handelskade beside the heart-shaped Punda Love Heart sculpture, with the two cannons nearby. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the heart or the pastel row over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Otrobanda end of the Queen Emma Bridge while you stand across the water on Handelskade, so the row of buildings sits behind you; late afternoon light is suggested.
card.rules_and_safety: Handelskade is a waterfront street, so it should be open to walk along, but check the official site before you go in case of events or closures.
card.challenge: Find a doorway, shutter or shop sign where two colours sit side by side, and snap it like it's a paint swatch.
card.good_to_know: Handelskade is a waterfront street in Willemstad, lined with a row of colourful buildings. You can walk to it from central Willemstad. The two cannons near the Punda Love Heart add a touch of naval history to your photo.

card.hook: This bright yellow building has been standing since 1732, and inside the floor is covered in sand. Outside, it's the easiest kind of subject: big, cheerful and hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Head for Hanchi di Snoa in Punda. The phone icon sits right on the building, so step out into the street and face the front, with the arched entrance in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural look at the whole front. If the street is too narrow to fit it all in, try 0.5x, but keep the building in the centre so the walls don't lean. Turn on gridlines and line the sides of the building up with them.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the yellow wall, then drag the brightness slider down a touch to make the picture darker if the sky is bright and the wall looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the light is softer and kinder to the yellow wall. Leave the flash off.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little higher than your face so the building fits behind you. Check the arched entrance isn't hidden behind your head.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship, so photos inside may be restricted, especially during services. Check the signs when you arrive. Photos are reportedly not allowed in the attached museum. Punda is busy, so watch for traffic while you frame your shot.
card.challenge: Get the arched entrance, a strip of blue sky and not a single parked car in one frame. Good luck!
card.good_to_know: Locals call it the Snoa. The congregation, Mikvé Israel-Emanuel, was founded in 1651 and the building was finished in 1732. It's described as the oldest surviving synagogue in the Americas and is still in use today. The interior is said to resemble the Portuguese Synagogue in Amsterdam.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Hanchi di Snoa in Punda. The phone icon sits right on the building, so step out into the street and face the front, with the arched entrance in the middle of your screen.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor can stand with the Curaçao Synagogue (Mikvé Israel-Emanuel, Hanchi di Snoa 29, Punda) directly behind them, so I am not reporting a selfie spot or a passer-by spot. The listings I found either skip the synagogue or are not photo spots for it. One guide puts a selfie in front of the big blue letters at Wilhelmina Park, which is not a synagogue backdrop (<cite index="2-1">the perfect spot to take a selfie while in Willemstad is in front of these giant blue letters at Wilhelmina Park</cite>). Another calls the Queen Emma Bridge a photo spot with colourful buildings behind it, and it is not near the synagogue as far as the page says (<cite index="7-3">it is a perfect photo spot because you have the colorful buildings in the background</cite>). The only synagogue-specific photo guidance is that the exterior is photogenic and the building is <cite index="12-1">very photogenic</cite>, but no page gives a standing point for a selfie or a photo of a visitor. On rules, the one photography restriction I found is about the building, not selfie sticks or tripods: <cite index="29-2">photography is allowed in the synagogue, but it is prohibited in the adjacent Jewish Cultural Historical Museum</cite>. The Atlas Obscura listing gives coordinates close to yours (12.105, -68.9325) for the same address. Checking the street with a local map or the museum staff would be the next step.

card.hook: Picture a quayside where boats bump gently against the wall, the stalls are a riot of colour, and everyone seems to be chatting at once. That's what you're looking for at the Floating Market in Willemstad.
card.stand_here: Start near Caprileskade, about 250 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From there you get one wide shot of the whole scene before you wander in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and use the gridlines to keep the water's edge level. If the row of boats and stalls won't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x, and keep it back from the edge because it stretches things near the corners. Then walk east, about 3 to 4 minutes on foot, to the quayside and use zoom 2x for produce, hands and faces.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest awning or piece of fruit, then slide the picture a little darker so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning is usually the liveliest time for a market, and the light is softer then. Try to skip the harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Sha Caprileskade quay beside the market boats and stalls, and stand by a boat or stall. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the colourful produce and boats over your shoulder. This spot is inferred from descriptions of the waterfront, so have a quick look on the ground first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot you from the Queen Wilhelmina Bridge (Wilhelminabrug), with the market's tarps, stalls and tethered boats along the Caprileskade waterfront below and behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working market, so photograph it after you've bought something and from a polite distance. Ask before taking close-ups of anyone.
card.challenge: Find the brightest colour in the whole market, then get a shot with it in the frame and its reflection in the water.
card.good_to_know: The Floating Market is in Willemstad, and the name tells you what to look for: stalls and boats at the water's edge, with produce for sale. What's open and where the boats tie up can change from day to day. Trading days and hours aren't confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near Caprileskade, about 250 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From there you get one wide shot of the whole scene before you wander in.

card.hook: Picture a row of painted buildings along the water, with one huge arch rising behind them like it's showing off. That's Queen Juliana Bridge from the Punda waterfront, and it's hard to take a bad photo of it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Handelskade on the Punda waterfront, near the pair of antique cannons. Face north across St. Anna Bay and the bridge will be right there in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the waterfront buildings and the whole arch in one go. Then switch to 1x for a tidier, more natural view, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the arch above the rooftops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower line so the bridge sits across the top, with the colourful buildings and water filling the bottom.
card.best_time: Morning or later in the afternoon gives softer light, so peek at how it's hitting the buildings before you settle in. Midday sun can flatten those lovely colours.
card.selfie_here: Try Fort Nassau, which sits near the bridge: use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the bridge behind you with the city below. Rif Fort also works, with the bridge behind you and colourful buildings in front.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the pair of antique cannons on Handelskade and ask a passer-by to stand on Handelskade facing you, so the bridge over Sint Anna Bay is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is an active roadway with no pedestrian walkway, so don't stop on it for photos. Stay on the waterfront and watch for passing traffic. The Rif Fort viewpoint is a hotel parking area, so check it's still open to visitors before you go.
card.challenge: Take the same shot at 0.5x, 1x and 2x, then pick your winner. Bonus points if the arch is dead straight against the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The bridge opened on 30 April 1974 and is named after Juliana of the Netherlands. It's a four-lane road bridge that stands 56.4 metres above the water at its highest point, so ships can pass into the narrow harbour. Once it was finished, the older Queen Emma Bridge closed to traffic and now carries only pedestrians.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Handelskade on the Punda waterfront, near the pair of antique cannons. Face north across St. Anna Bay and the bridge will be right there in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a country house painted bright yellow, with flowers lined up along the front like they're waiting for their photo too. That's Landhuis Chobolobo, and "landhuis" is just the Dutch word for country house.
card.stand_here: Walk to the phone icon near Junostraat, about 25 m south-east of the house (roughly 1 minute on foot from the map app's drop-off). Face north-west and keep the house roughly in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole house. If you're close and want more of the building and the sky, drop to 0.5x, but keep the house in the centre so the edges don't stretch. Then use zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out details without walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the walls up with the vertical lines so the house stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is kinder to the colours. Midday light is harsh and the shadows are short.
card.selfie_here: Head for the grounds in front of the yellow façade, where the flowers are planted along the front. Use the front camera, step back a little and let the bright yellow wall fill the space behind your shoulder. The courtyard near the cocktail bar is a cosy, shaded alternative, but check on arrival that the house is actually behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the grounds in front of the mansion and ask a passer-by to shoot from the phone icon, facing north-west, so the whole house fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Check current access before you go, and stay on open or public ground if you step closer.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole house, then find three close-up details, such as a window, a doorway or a bit of wall, and see if a friend can guess where each one is.
card.good_to_know: A landhuis is the Dutch name for a country house. Chobolobo is known as the home of the genuine Blue Curaçao liqueur. It sits in the Saliña area of Willemstad.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the phone icon near Junostraat, about 25 m south-east of the house (roughly 1 minute on foot from the map app's drop-off). Face north-west and keep the house roughly in the middle of your screen.

card.hook: Picture a whole street of houses painted like a box of sweets, with giant murals next door. That's Bargestraat, and it's hard to take a dull photo here.
card.stand_here: Head for Bargestraat in Scharloo, about 350 m to the east, a short walk of around 4 to 5 minutes. Stand on the public pavement and face the row of brightly painted houses and murals.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole street in. Switch to 1x for a single house or mural, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for balconies, gables or the two birds on the Dare building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the house fronts up with them, then tap the brightest wall and slide a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the facades and the colours look warmer.
card.selfie_here: On Bargestraat, use the front camera at 0.5x and pose in front of the murals or the bright houses so they frame you. The Dare building, on a prominent street corner with the Three O'Clock Romance mural, also makes a bold backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the street from the green mansion nicknamed the Wedding Cake, so they can fit the whole facade in with you in front (check the exact spot on the map when you arrive).
card.rules_and_safety: Frame your shots from the public pavement. One review says Scharloo isn't a place to walk around at night, while daytime visits are considered safe.
card.challenge: Find the Dare building and get both painted birds in one shot, with you looking suitably smug in the corner.
card.good_to_know: Scharloo began in 1634 as a Dutch West Indies Company plantation, but the soil was poor and it was soon abandoned. From 1870 wealthy Jewish merchants built villas here, and the area has been part of the UNESCO-listed historic centre since 1999. Murals can be repainted or covered, so treat what you see on arrival as the current version.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Bargestraat in Scharloo, about 350 m to the east, a short walk of around 4 to 5 minutes. Stand on the public pavement and face the row of brightly painted houses and murals.

card.hook: Here's a fun twist: to get the best picture of one fort, you stand on its twin. The Waterfort's long, heavy wall rises straight out of the water, and the view across the harbour mouth is the one you'll want.
card.stand_here: Walk up onto the ramparts of Rif Fort, on the western side of the channel, and stop on the open walls rather than heading into the shops or restaurants. Face south-east across the water and the Waterfort and the Punda waterfront are right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the fort wall and the waterfront together. Go to zoom 0.5x for more water and sky, or zoom 2x to pick out the wall and the waterfront buildings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the horizon level, and tap the fort wall; if the sky is glaring, slide it a little darker so the stone and colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or around sunset is the time to aim for.
card.selfie_here: Try the ocean-facing terrace at the Waterfort Arches restaurant row, Waterfortstraat 41 on Plasa Piar, beside Fort Amsterdam. It's described as a photogenic waterfront terrace facing the sea, so use the front camera, zoom 0.5x, and hold it out so the arches and the fort setting fit in behind you.
card.ask_someone: On Plasa Piar, the square next to the Waterfort, ask a passer-by to take your photo from a spot where the fort walls are in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The hotel fills the inside of the fort, so photograph it from the outside, from the walls or the quay. Wall and quay access can be restricted at times, so check the official site first. One photo guide says the quay on the sea side is regularly flooded and slippery with algae (it may be out of date), so watch your step.
card.challenge: Can you get the fort wall sitting neatly on the lower third of your screen, with a bit of Rif Fort's rampart edge in the corner to show you're shooting from another fort?
card.good_to_know: The Waterfort was built from 1827 to guard the town, and a twin fort, Rif Fort, was planned for the opposite bank. Marines were stationed here from 1858. In 1955 the Plaza Hotel Curaçao was built inside the walls, which is why you see old fortification and a working hotel in one place today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk up onto the ramparts of Rif Fort, on the western side of the channel, and stop on the open walls rather than heading into the shops or restaurants. Face south-east across the water and the Waterfort and the Punda waterfront are right in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a channel so wide it splits a whole town in two, with Punda on one bank and Otrobanda on the other. Then a boat slides through and suddenly the whole scene makes sense.
card.stand_here: Head for the spot near De Rouvilleweg and stand about 200 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, then face north-east. Walk a little closer if you want the channel to fill more of the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the channel, both banks and loads of sky in one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single boat or a bit of the far bank.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a lower or upper line so it sits level, and let the water's edge lead the eye down the channel.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and a more comfortable walk, and sunrise is a nice bet for views toward Punda. Around midday the sun is high and the water can look flat and glary.
card.selfie_here: Try the Handelskade waterfront in Punda: stand in front of the row of colourful colonial houses with the water behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to squeeze more in, and hold your phone a little higher.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Queen Emma Bridge (Pontjesbrug) on the Punda side while you stand in front of the Handelskade houses, so the bay and the whole row fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Walking across the Queen Juliana Bridge isn't permitted, as it's only for driving over, so skip it for photos. The Queen Emma Bridge opens regularly for ships, so check for openings before you head there.
card.challenge: Be patient and wait for a boat to glide into your frame, then grab one wide shot and one tighter shot of it at 2x or more.
card.good_to_know: Sint Anna Bay is about a mile long and up to 1,000 feet wide. It opens into the Caribbean Sea at the southern end and leads into the Schottegat, the big inner lagoon and industrial area, at the northern end. Sea air can leave a film on your phone's camera, so give it a wipe before you start.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the spot near De Rouvilleweg and stand about 200 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, then face north-east. Walk a little closer if you want the channel to fill more of the frame.
